c.tagline: Imperial capital where dynasties meet modern China.

emergency.note: Fire is 119 and traffic police 122; English-speaking operators are rare, so have a local or your hotel call for you.

hood_landmark.Dongcheng: The Forbidden City and Tiananmen Square
hood_landmark.Xicheng: Beihai Park's white dagoba and the Houhai lakes
hood_landmark.Haidian: The Summer Palace's lake, gardens and pavilions
hood_landmark.Sanlitun: Taikoo Li's open-air shopping, bars and nightlife

avoid.reason: The "tea house"/art-student and rickshaw scams around Wangfujing/Tiananmen; pickpocketing in crowds

hood_desc: Dongcheng is the historic heart of Beijing, home to the Forbidden City, Temple of Heaven, and atmospheric hutong alleys; ideal for first-time visitors and history or culture lovers who want to be steps from the main sights.

Xicheng covers the old citys western half with Beihai Park, the Houhai lake district, and Financial Street; it suits travelers wanting traditional courtyard charm, lakeside strolls, and lively evening bars away from the tourist crush.

Chaoyang is Beijings sprawling modern district, packed with the CBD skyline, embassies, malls, and international dining; best for business travelers, expats, and anyone who prefers a cosmopolitan, convenient base.

Haidian is the northwestern university and tech hub, anchored by Tsinghua and Peking universities, the Zhongguancun tech zone, and the Summer Palace; a good fit for students, families, and visitors drawn to greenery and academia.

Sanlitun, inside Chaoyang, is the citys nightlife and fashion epicenter with Taikoo Li shopping, rooftop bars, and clubs; ideal for young travelers and anyone chasing shopping, dining, and a buzzing after-dark scene.

water.note: Avoid tap water; stick to bottled or boiled water, which is the local norm even for residents.

transit.pay: Use the reloadable Yikatong card, sold and topped up at station counters and vending machines, or the Yikatong app for phone tap-in. Since late 2024, all subway lines and city buses also accept tap-to-pay with foreign Visa and Mastercard contactless cards. Subway fares are distance-based, starting at ¥3 (about $0.40) up to 6 km and rising to roughly ¥6-10 for cross-town rides; buses are typically ¥1-2.
transit.hours: Most subway lines run about 5-5:30am to 11-11:30pm, sometimes extended on major holidays; the dense bus network includes night-bus routes running through the early morning.

landmarks: Great Wall of China (Badaling)
The most-visited section of the ancient Great Wall, snaking dramatically across mountain ridges near Beijing.
Forbidden City
The vast imperial palace complex of Ming and Qing emperors, famed for its red walls, golden roofs, and grand courtyards.
Tiananmen Square
One of the largest public squares in the world, flanked by Mao's portrait gate and major national monuments.
Temple of Heaven
A masterpiece of Ming-dynasty religious architecture, its circular triple-gabled hall is instantly recognizable.
Summer Palace
An imperial garden retreat centered on Kunming Lake and Longevity Hill, exquisite for reflective lake photography.
Beijing National Stadium (Bird's Nest)
The striking lattice-steel 2008 Olympic stadium, a modern architectural icon of the city.
Lama Temple (Yonghegong)
Beijing's largest and most active Tibetan Buddhist temple, rich with colorful halls and incense-filled courtyards.
Beijing Hutongs
Historic narrow alleyways of traditional courtyard housing, offering an atmospheric glimpse of old Beijing life.
Beihai Park
A serene imperial garden park centered on a lake and the striking white Tibetan-style pagoda on Jade Island.
798 Art District
A former Bauhaus-style munitions factory turned sprawling contemporary art zone, with galleries, studios, sculpture and cafes filling its converted industrial halls.

intl.op: China Railway (train K23, via Mongolian Railway UBTZ)

train.note: The weekly K23 sleeper to Ulaanbaatar (departs Tue) is the main international train running in 2026; international tickets can't be bought on the 12306 website and are sold at the Beijing International Hotel ticket office or through agents. The Beijing-Moscow Trans-Mongolian (K3) and Trans-Manchurian (K19) sleepers remain suspended. The K27 to Pyongyang resumed in March 2026, but independent travel to North Korea is heavily restricted. Domestic high-speed and sleeper trains from Beijing's stations (including through high-speed services to Hong Kong West Kowloon) reach the whole country - book on 12306 with your passport.

bus.note: No scheduled international coaches run from Beijing. Long-distance domestic buses leave from terminals such as Liuliqiao and Sihui, with frequent departures to Chengde (every 20 minutes, about ¥70) and other cities in Hebei, but for almost every trip the train is faster and simpler to book.

ferry.note: Beijing is inland and has no ferries. The nearest sea crossings leave from Tianjin (about 1.5h away by high-speed train); ferries from Tianjin to Incheon (South Korea) have run intermittently, so check the operator before relying on them.
